Aerial Wildlife 
Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 516 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018) 
 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit 516 (WMU 516) covers an area of 3,979 km 2, with 2,644 km2 comprising caribou range 
and 219 km2 designated as a Key Wildlife and Biodiversity Zone. The WMU is delineated by the 21st baseline 
(latitude 55 degrees 59 minutes) in the north, the Athabasca River to the east, the confluence of the Calling River 
and Athabasca River to the south, and in the west by the Calling River and Secondary Highway 813. The northern 
boreal mixedwood forest is the predominant ecoregion in the WMU, with a smaller portion of the lower foothills 
region also represented. Sandy, Pelican and Rock Island lakes are the largest waterbodies, each with an area less 
than 30 km2. First Nations reserves present in WMU 516 include Bigstone Cree Nation (Wabasca No.166A) . 
A survey for moose (Alces alces) and white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) was last conducted for WMU 516 
in 2011 using the random stratified block methodology (Random Block). The moose population was estimated to 
have 933 individuals, a density of 0.26 moose/km 2, and a bull:cow:calf ratio of 32:100:45 (Norstrom and Ranger 
2011). See Table 1 for previous moose survey estimates for WMU 516 and surrounding WMUs. Hunting 
regulations for 2017 allowed for antlered moose to be harvested during an Archery Only Season (August 25 – 31), 
and a split General Season with Special Licences (September 1- October 31 or November 1 – November 30). The 
white-tailed deer population was estimated to have 1856 individuals and a density of 0.49 white-tailed deer/km2 
(Norstrom and Ranger 2011). See Table 2 for a comparison of white-tailed deer survey estimates. Hunting 
regulations for 2017 allowed for antlered and antlerless white-tailed deer to be harvested during an Archery Only 
Season (August 25 – 31) and a General Season (September 1– November 30). A Supplemental Antlerless White-
tailed Deer Licence was available for WMU 516. 
The objective of the 2018 survey was to assess the status of the moose and white -tailed deer population in WMU 
516 by determining estimates for abundance, density and the age-sex composition. 
 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for ungulates was conducted February 1 st to 4th, 2018 using distance sampling techniques 
(Buckland et al., 2001, 2010). A total of 187 east-west transect lines (survey effort = 1,595 km) were flown. Moose 
were classified by age class (adult or calf) and sex. Other wildlife sightings were recorded.  
 
Results 
A total of 105 moose were observed in 66 groups, which included; 56 cows, 27 calves, 21 bulls (16 antlerless and 
5 with antlers), and 1 unclassified adult. The encounter rate was 0.04 moose/km2 (90% confidence interval (CI) of 
0.03 – 0.05). The estimated density was 0.08 moose/km2 (90% CI 0.06 – 0.10) and the estimated abundance was

313 individuals (90% CI 248 – 396). The coefficient of variation for both density and abundance was 0.14 (Table 
3). A total of 104 moose were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf rat io was estimated to be 38:100:48. 
 
For white-tailed deer, 88 were observed in 38 groups. The encounter rate was 0.02 white -tailed deer/km2 (90% 
confidence interval (CI) of 0.02 – 0.03). The estimated density was 0.14 white-tailed deer/km2 (90% CI 0.09 – 0.20) 
and the estimated abundance was 564 individuals (90% CI 393 – 808). The coefficient of variation for both density 
and abundance was 0.22 (Table 3). Attempts were not made to classify, however 15 does, 18 fawns and 55 
unclassified white-tailed deer were noted.
